progression.prerequisiteKnowledge: bio-m8-b05 (transpiration: water evaporates inside the leaf and diffuses out as vapour, mostly through stomata, mostly on the underside; xylem carries water up; hot, dry, windy air speeds the loss because wind removes the moist air at the leaf surface; guard cells and ABA), bio-m8-g03 (feedback loop practice; not needed here beyond b05's loop), Year 11 diffusion and xylem. From Module 7 practicals (bio-m7-p02, bio-m7-p05): aim, independent, dependent and controlled variables, a control, repeats and a risk table as a format. Not assumed: potometer, stomatal peel, field of view counting, the VRA words as s07 defines them (s07 comes next in the Biology playlist; this video uses its three plain questions without teaching the target picture). Start: set a controlled comparison of water uptake by one leafy shoot in still and moving air. Stop: interpret the uptake data and its limits (uptake is not loss; one cut shoot is not a plant in a paddock; a stomatal count shows where water can leave, not how fast). Next handoff: skills-s07, "Practical questions: validity, reliability, accuracy and fixes that fix" (route review change 10), then bio-m8-b06.
progression.startsWith: You can't see water vapour leaving a leaf. But you can watch a tiny air bubble creep along a glass tube as a leafy shoot draws water in. In still air, it moves about four millimetres a minute. With a fan on, it moves more than twice as fast. So how do you test this fairly, and what does the bubble really tell you?
progression.stopsAfter: explaining why water uptake by a leafy shoot tracks its water loss; naming the parts of a bubble potometer and why the bubble moves; setting it up airtight (cut and fit under water, sealed joints, dry leaves, settled shoot) with a reason for each; stating the aim and variables for an air movement comparison on one shoot; using still air as the control and three timed readings per condition; calculating a rate (distance ÷ time) and a mean; judging the spread against the gap; concluding narrowly and explaining the result with b05's boundary layer reason; naming the limits (uptake is not loss; one cut shoot; a desk fan); describing a stomatal count with a nail varnish peel and what it can and cannot show; judging validity, reliability and accuracy; writing a three-row risk assessment; calculating and explaining a humidity comparison; identifying and fixing two problems in a flawed method.
progression.nextLesson: practical questions in depth, validity, reliability, accuracy and fixes that fix (skills-s07, route review change 10), then what causes a non-infectious disease (bio-m8-b06).

teaching.task: You can't see water vapour leaving a leaf. How do you measure a plant's water loss fairly, and what can that measurement really tell you?
teaching.causalExplanation: (1) the bubble puzzle; (2) why uptake tracks loss (b05 recall: loss at the leaves pulls water up); (3) the potometer's parts and why the bubble moves; (4) why airtight, why cut under water, why dry leaves, why settle; (5) aim and variables, one shoot so leaf area cannot change; (6) still air as the control, three timed readings, settle after a change; (7) one worked rate (21 ÷ 5 = 4.2), reading the same bubble edge at eye level; (8) results, means, spread against gap, the conclusion and its b05 reason; (9) what the bubble cannot tell you; (10) stomatal count as a second method, and its own limit; (11) VRA; (12) risk; attempts; decision rule and handoff; key notes.
teaching.conversationalApproach: You can't see water vapour leaving a leaf. Recall how plants lose water. That's the job of a potometer, a device that measures how fast a shoot takes up water. Any leak means the bubble no longer tracks what the shoot takes in, so the set-up must be airtight. The aim: find out how air movement affects the rate of water uptake by a leafy shoot. Still air is the control, the comparison without the fan. Here's one reading. Here are all six. Be careful what you claim. A second method asks a different question: where can water leave? Paint clear nail varnish on a leaf, let it dry, and lift it off with clear tape. Now judge it with three questions. The risk assessment. Your turn. Thirty divided by six is five millimetres per minute without the bag, and twelve divided by six is two with it. One more. One: cutting in air lets air into the xylem, which can block uptake, so cut and fit the shoot under water. So for any transpiration practical: change one factor, keep everything else the same, seal it airtight, repeat each reading, and claim only what you measured, the uptake by this shoot.
teaching.openingDecision: You can't see water vapour leaving a leaf. But you can watch a tiny air bubble creep along a glass tube as a leafy shoot draws water in. In still air, it moves about four millimetres a minute. With a fan on, it moves more than twice as fast. So how do you test this fairly, and what does the bubble really tell you?
teaching.understandingCheck: - (A1, calculate and explain, 4 marks) One shoot, potometer, with and without a clear plastic bag sealed around the stem below the leaves; 30 mm in 6 min without, 12 mm in 6 min with. (a) Calculate both rates (5.0 and 2.0 mm min⁻¹). (b) Explain the difference: water vapour from the leaves builds up inside the bag, the air around the leaves becomes very humid, the water vapour difference between the inside of the leaf and the air is smaller, so vapour diffuses out more slowly and the shoot takes up less water. Crossed mistake: "the bag blocks the water" (it traps humid air; the stomata are not covered). Unseen: humidity, not air movement; numbers differ from the worked data and from the site's Year 11 potometer page (18 mm in 6 min, 40 mm in 5 min).
teaching.curriculumScope: Scope: a practical video for the "investigate" half of B8-IQ1-02 (plant water balance). It follows the Biology practical format and voice of `bio-m7-p05.md` (Revision 3: three-zone board, method step rail, one card at a time, painted bench objects, no hands, VRA cards, a risk table that shows only the spoken row, two attempts, key notes) and the answer language of `skills-s07.md` (validity, reliability and accuracy as three plain questions; word, feature, fix; repeats help reliability but cannot fix an uncontrolled variable).
